launch_app.description: Launch an installed app by 16-hex-character product_id. Ids come from the App List action (X_GetAppList); the App entity below carries the widely-deployed subset as static options because the action's reply is a flat string, not XML elements an options_source could walk.

product_id.description: 16 hex characters from X_GetAppList, e.g. "0010000200000001" for Netflix.

press_apps.description: Open the apps list. keys.py spells this NRC_APPS; Home Assistant's docs list the same name as undocumented-but-working.

press_exit.description: Exit the current menu or app.

press_home.description: Viera home screen (My Home Screen on 2019+ sets).

press_input_hdmi1.description: Switch directly to HDMI 1 (undocumented key, per Home Assistant docs).

press_input_toggle.description: Cycle to the next AV input (the INPUT/AV key).

press_input_tuner.description: Switch to the antenna/tuner (the TV key).

press_last_view.description: Switch back to the previously viewed channel.

press_option.description: Option key — context menu / pin to home (NRC_SUBMENU on the wire).

press_power.description: Power toggle. Network wake needs network standby enabled on the TV (see above).

set_mute_off.description: Unmute via DMR RenderingControl. Plain SOAP on both generations.

set_mute_on.description: Mute via DMR RenderingControl (discrete, unlike the NRC_MUTE toggle key). Plain SOAP on both generations.

set_volume.description: Set absolute volume 0-100 via DMR RenderingControl. Plain SOAP on both TV generations.

volume.description: 0-100. panasonic-viera rejects values outside that range client-side; the library types it int, rendered here as the XML text.

identity.notes: UDNs observed on Viera sets start "uuid:4D454930-" (4D454930 is ASCII "MEI0"); Home Assistant uses the UDN as its unique id, so a client should too. The sets also answer ssdp:all and upnp:rootdevice, but the p00RemoteController:1 search target is the identifying signal.

device.name: Panasonic Viera Network Remote Control
device.notes: Panasonic Viera smart TVs expose a UPnP-style SOAP API on port 55000 with no authentication on pre-2019 sets. Discovery is SSDP M-SEARCH for urn:panasonic-com:device:p00RemoteController:1; the LOCATION header points at http://<ip>:55000/nrc/ddd.xml, the device description that carries UDN, friendlyName and modelNumber. Control is POST /nrc/control_0 with service urn:panasonic-com:service:p00NetworkControl:1: X_SendKey takes an X_KeyEvent argument of NRC_*-ONOFF key names (one SOAP call per button press-and-release), X_GetVectorInfo and X_GetAppList query state, and X_LaunchApp starts apps by product_id. Absolute volume and mute live on a standard UPnP DMR RenderingControl service at /dmr/control_0. From circa 2019 the NRC service requires PIN pairing and AES-encrypted commands; the sets advertise this by listing X_GetEncryptSessionId in their service description at /nrc/sdd_0.xml. Power-on over the network works only from network standby — enable it on the TV under Settings > Network > TV Remote App Settings ("Powered On By Apps" / "Networked Standby"); otherwise use Wake-on-LAN. Several older plasma models on the Home Assistant supported list are noted as unable to power on over the network at all.

openness.notes: Panasonic never published this API. Every byte documented here was recovered by the community — the 2019+ encryption was reverse engineered out of the official app's libtvconnect.so (see panasonic-viera issue #9) — so nothing upstream is authoritative.

issued_to_client: X_Keyword — base64 16-byte key the session AES/HMAC keys derive from (encrypted models)
credentials.notes: Pre-2019 sets have no access control at all: anything that can route to port 55000 can drive the TV. On encrypted models the issued X_ApplicationId/X_Keyword pair is the whole credential — store both and treat the keyword as a secret.

factory_reset.effect: Clears network credentials, paired clients, account link, apps and settings; the TV returns to first-run setup.

steps.action: Menu > Setup > System Menu > Factory Defaults (some model years: 'Shipping Condition').
steps.notes: Menu path varies by generation and region; taken from Panasonic manual conventions, not verified here against a specific model's manual.

methods.description: First-run setup on the TV with the bundled remote: language, network selection (WiFi passphrase entry or Ethernet), then on smart models a Viera account prompt that gates app store features, not the NRC API. Afterwards confirm network remote control is enabled — Settings > Network > TV Remote App Settings — and, if power-on-over-LAN is wanted, enable "Powered On By Apps" / "Networked Standby" in the same menu (naming varies by model year).

steps.action: Power on the TV and complete the on-screen setup with the remote.
Join the WiFi network (or connect Ethernet) on the TV itself.
Enable network remote control under Settings > Network > TV Remote App Settings.
steps.notes: Naming varies by model year; on some sets this is on by default.

steps.action: Confirm the NRC API is reachable from the LAN.
On encrypted sets, run the PIN pairing from nrc_common.encrypted_session.
steps.expect: Stored X_ApplicationId and X_Keyword (encryption key); TV shows a pairing-complete message.

request.action: X_DisplayPinCode, then X_RequestAuth with the on-screen PIN

methods.description: Pre-2019 sets: nothing further — X_SendKey works from any LAN host with no credentials. Detect the generation by fetching /nrc/sdd_0.xml and looking for the X_GetEncryptSessionId action (its presence means pairing is required), which is exactly what the panasonic-viera library does.

setup.notes: TV onboarding is entirely on the TV's own screen; there is no app-driven provisioning to reimplement. The NRC API itself needs no pairing on pre-2019 sets — it is open to every host on the LAN once the TV is on the network. On circa-2019-and-later sets a one-time client pairing is required instead: the client asks the TV to show a 4-digit PIN, submits it, and receives an application id and encryption key it must store and reuse (the full flow is in nrc_common.encrypted_session). Pairing is per client, not per network: re-pair only if the stored credentials are lost or the TV is factory reset.

rejoin.notes: Re-running the network setup from the TV's settings menu changes only the network; a factory reset is never needed just to change routers.

http_endpoints.description: UPnP device description: deviceType urn:panasonic-com:device:p00RemoteController:1, friendlyName, manufacturer, modelName, modelNumber, UDN. This is the identity document discovery parses; Home Assistant keys its config entry on the UDN. Open on both generations, no auth.
http_endpoints.name: Device Description

http_endpoints.description: SCPD for the NRC service. Its actionList is the generation detector: X_GetEncryptSessionId present means the 2019+ PIN + AES pairing is required (nrc_common.encrypted_session); absent means plain SOAP.
http_endpoints.name: NRC Service Description

http_endpoints.description: Action X_SendKey, argument <X_KeyEvent>NRC_*-ONOFF</X_KeyEvent>: one press-and-release of a remote key. Some firmware generations expose the same function as X_RemoteControl instead — same argument, same effect; check /nrc/sdd_0.xml. The `commands` block names one invocation per key. Replies are an empty X_SendKeyResponse on success.
http_endpoints.name: Send Key

http_endpoints.description: Action X_GetVectorInfo, no arguments; answers X_NewVectorInfo, a Panasonic-internal device/node identification string. Kept for completeness — discovery gets everything it needs from ddd.xml.
http_endpoints.name: Vector Info

http_endpoints.description: Action X_GetAppList, no arguments; answers X_AppList, a flat quote-delimited string of 'vc_app' entries each carrying product_id=<16 hex chars> and a display name (panasonic-viera parses it with regex, not XML). Not usable as a select's options_source — the options_source contract wants one XML element per option — which is why the App entity below carries a static table instead.
http_endpoints.name: App List

http_endpoints.description: Action X_LaunchApp with <X_AppType>vc_app</X_AppType> and <X_LaunchKeyword>product_id={product_id}</X_LaunchKeyword> (or resource_id={n} for built-in functions — resource_id 1063 opens the web browser). Launches an installed app by the product_id the App List action returns.
http_endpoints.name: Launch App

http_endpoints.description: Action X_DisplayPinCode, argument <X_DeviceName>{client name}</X_DeviceName>: pairing step 1 on 2019+ sets. TV shows a 4-digit PIN; response carries the X_ChallengeKey. See nrc_common.encrypted_session.pairing.
http_endpoints.name: Display PIN Code

http_endpoints.description: Action X_RequestAuth, argument <X_AuthInfo>{encrypted PIN}</X_AuthInfo>: pairing step 2. Error code 600 = wrong PIN. Success returns X_AuthResult holding the X_ApplicationId/X_Keyword credentials.
http_endpoints.name: Request Auth

http_endpoints.description: Action X_GetEncryptSessionId: opens an encrypted session for stored credentials and returns the X_SessionId every X_EncryptedCommand needs. See nrc_common.encrypted_session.session.
http_endpoints.name: Get Encrypt Session Id

http_endpoints.description: Action X_EncryptedCommand: the wrapper every other NRC action rides in on 2019+ sets, with X_ApplicationId and X_EncInfo arguments. Envelope construction is in nrc_common.encrypted_session.command_envelope.
http_endpoints.name: Encrypted Command

http_endpoints.description: Standard UPnP RenderingControl GetVolume (InstanceID 0, Channel Master); answers CurrentVolume, 0-100. Plain SOAP on BOTH generations — the 2019+ encryption wraps only the NRC service.
http_endpoints.name: Get Volume

http_endpoints.description: RenderingControl SetVolume with DesiredVolume 0-100. Plain SOAP on both generations.
http_endpoints.name: Set Volume

http_endpoints.description: RenderingControl GetMute; answers CurrentMute 0/1. Plain SOAP on both generations.
http_endpoints.name: Get Mute

http_endpoints.description: RenderingControl SetMute with DesiredMute 0/1. Plain SOAP on both generations.
http_endpoints.name: Set Mute

encrypted_session.applies_to: Sets whose /nrc/sdd_0.xml actionList contains X_GetEncryptSessionId — circa 2019 and later (FZ/GZ/HZ/JZ and onward). Detect at runtime exactly this way; do not guess from the model string.

command_envelope.description: How every NRC command (X_SendKey, X_GetVectorInfo, X_LaunchApp, ...) travels on an encrypted set. The three pairing/session actions above are the only ones sent plain.
command_envelope.template: Build "<X_SessionId>{session_id}</X_SessionId>" + "<X_SequenceNumber>{seq as 8-digit zero-padded decimal}</X_SequenceNumber>" + "<X_OriginalCommand><u:{action} xmlns:u=\"urn:panasonic-com:service:p00NetworkControl:1\">{arguments}</u:{action}></X_OriginalCommand>", encrypt it per payload_encoding with the session keys, then send the plain action X_EncryptedCommand with arguments <X_ApplicationId>{app_id}</X_ApplicationId><X_EncInfo>{encrypted}</X_EncInfo>. The reply's X_EncResult decrypts the same way and contains the command's real <Action>Response fragment.

encrypted_session.evidence: reported — panasonic-viera remote_control.py and the LogicMachine Lua port agree byte for byte; the mask constant comes from the official app's libtvconnect.so (panasonic-viera issue #9).

pairing.description: One-time. Yields the two credentials device.setup.credentials.issued_to_client names; store both and never pair again unless they are lost.

steps.action: Send X_DisplayPinCode with argument <X_DeviceName>{client name}</X_DeviceName>. The TV overlays a 4-digit PIN on its screen. Response carries X_ChallengeKey, base64 of a 16-byte challenge — this challenge IS the pairing IV.
Read the 4-digit PIN off the TV screen and hand it to the client.

Derive the pairing keys from the challenge IV. AES key: process the IV in 4-byte groups, emitting each group REVERSED and with each byte bitwise-NOTed (key[4g..4g+3] = ~iv[4g+3], ~iv[4g+2], ~iv[4g+1], ~iv[4g]). HMAC key (32 bytes): the constant mask 15 C9 5A C2 B0 8A A7 EB 4E 22 8F 81 1E 34 D0 4F A5 4B A7 DC AC 98 79 FA 8A CD A3 FC 24 4F 38 54 XORed against the IV with a per-position rotation, exactly as panasonic-viera's authorize_pin_code implements it: stepping i by 4, hmac[i] = mask[i] XOR iv[(i+2)&0xF], hmac[i+1] = mask[i+1] XOR iv[(i+3)&0xF], hmac[i+2] = mask[i+2] XOR iv[i&0xF], hmac[i+3] = mask[i+3] XOR iv[(i+1)&0xF]. Encrypt "<X_PinCode>{pin}</X_PinCode>" per payload_encoding and send it as <X_AuthInfo>{encrypted}</X_AuthInfo> to X_RequestAuth.
steps.expect: HTTP 500 / errorCode 600 means a wrong PIN.

steps.action: Decrypt the X_AuthResult return value with the same pairing keys; inside is <X_ApplicationId> and <X_Keyword>. Store both. The keyword is base64 of 16 bytes that anchor every later session.

encrypted_session.payload_encoding: Every encrypted argument shares one encoding, used in both directions. Plaintext: a 16-byte header (12 random bytes, then the 4-byte big-endian length of the following XML fragment) followed by the XML fragment itself, zero-padded to a multiple of 16 bytes. Encrypt with AES-128-CBC (zero padding, i.e. none added beyond the zero pad). Append the HMAC-SHA-256 of the ciphertext, keyed with the HMAC key. Base64 the concatenation — that string is what rides inside the XML argument. Decryption reverses it: base64-decode, split off the trailing 32-byte HMAC, AES-decrypt, skip the 16-byte header, cut at the first NUL.

session.description: Run once per client process start (credentials already stored).

steps.action: Derive the session keys from base64-decoded X_Keyword. IV: the keyword bytes themselves. AES key: each 4-byte group SWAPPED in pairs (key[4g..4g+3] = iv[4g+2], iv[4g+3], iv[4g], iv[4g+1]) — no NOT this time; the pairing and session derivations differ and mixing them up is the classic implementation bug. HMAC key: the IV bytes concatenated twice (32 bytes).

Encrypt "<X_ApplicationId>{app_id}</X_ApplicationId>" with the session keys and send X_GetEncryptSessionId with <X_ApplicationId>{app_id}</X_ApplicationId><X_EncInfo>{encrypted}</X_EncInfo>. Decrypt the X_EncResult reply; inside is <X_SessionId>.
Set a per-session sequence counter to 1. It increments on every successful command and rolls nothing back on transport errors (panasonic-viera decrements it again if the POST itself fails).

encrypted_session.transport_gap: NOT SUPPORTED by the reference app's `soap` transport today: the transport renders plain envelopes, while this generation needs AES-128-CBC encryption, HMAC-SHA-256, base64, a persistent sequence counter and stored credentials around every NRC command. A consumer must implement the flow below as a wrapper around the same SOAP POST; the DMR volume service stays plain and works on both generations.

request_format.argument_qualification: Action arguments are UNQUALIFIED: send <X_KeyEvent>...</X_KeyEvent>, with the xmlns:u declared ON THE ACTION ELEMENT. Same convention as Wemo, and the same XML-library caveat applies.
request_format.description: Everything needed to build a plain (pre-2019) Viera SOAP request byte for byte. All NRC actions go to one URL; the action is chosen by the SOAPACTION header and the body's action element.

example.description: X_SendKey pressing the Home key, as it goes on the wire.

headers.SOAPACTION: "urn:panasonic-com:service:p00NetworkControl:1#<Action>"  (literal double quotes are part of the value)

response_format.description: Standard UPnP SOAP: the Body's single child is <Action>Response, its children the named return values (X_GetVectorInfo answers X_NewVectorInfo, X_GetAppList answers X_AppList). A Body child named Fault is an error; the TV answers HTTP 500 with an errorCode element (600 = invalid PIN during pairing).

errors.http_500_soap_fault: Error responses are HTTP 500 carrying a SOAP Fault with errorCode and errorDescription elements — do not treat the HTTP status alone as a transport failure.

dmr.notes: A standard UPnP AV RenderingControl endpoint: absolute volume 0-100 and boolean mute on InstanceID 0, Channel Master. Useful alongside the NRC step keys because it can READ the level back.

nrc.notes: X_SendKey and X_RemoteControl both take <X_KeyEvent>NRC_*-ONOFF</X_KeyEvent> and press a key; different firmware generations expose one, the other, or both — the panasonic-viera library sends X_SendKey, older community write-ups use X_RemoteControl. Take the real action list from the set's own SCPD at /nrc/sdd_0.xml rather than assuming either. The X_GetEncryptSessionId/X_DisplayPinCode/X_RequestAuth/X_EncryptedCommand quartet appears only on the 2019+ encrypted generation.
